title: Wenyi Wang
text:
Welcome to my personal website. This is Wenyi Wang, a PhD student in Criminology, School of Economic, Political and Policy Sciences (EPPS), University of Texas at Dallas.
Quantitative criminologist studying how vice market legalization shapes behavioral harm, crime, and inequality among vulnerable populations.

title: Wenyi Wang
text:
Areas of Specialization

Gambling, Vice Markets, and Regulation: causal effects of gambling expansion on crime and harm; spatial analysis on exposure to gambling products and behavioral harm; translational criminology and evidence-based public policy
Quantitative Methods and Causal Inference: quasi-experimental and survey experiment for policy evaluation, Bayesian models for sparse and zero-inflated outcomes, hierarchical longitudinal modeling for longitudinal data analysis

title: Assignment 2: Google Trends, Two Ways
text:
Data sheet: primary website query



Terms: Trump, Kamala Harris, Election (each selected as a search term, not a topic)
Geography: United States (US) · Window: past five years (today+5-y)
Category: all (0) · Search type: Web Search (web)
Pulled: 2026-09-12 16:38:24 CDT
Query: Google Trends Explore
The website CSV covers 2021-09-12 through 2026-09-06 at weekly intervals. With the same three terms but a 90-day window, the CSV covers 2026-06-12 through 2026-09-12 daily. Thus, Google changed the time resolution with the window. My additional current-news term was Federal Reserve (US, past 90 days, all categories, Web Search), pulled 2026-09-12 16:39:35 CDT; the term was timely because an FOMC meeting was scheduled for September 15–16 (Federal Reserve calendar).

title: Assignment 2: Google Trends, Two Ways
text:
R pull and comparison


Code
library(gtrendsR)
library(readr)

r_pull <- gtrends(
  c("Trump", "Kamala Harris", "Election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE, geo = "US", gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y", category = 0
)
write_csv(r_pull$interest_over_time,
          "data/r_trump_kamala-election_us_5y_2026-09-12.csv")




Code
ggplot(web, aes(date, hits, color = keyword)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.55) +
  geom_point(data = r |> group_by(keyword) |> slice(seq(1, n(), by = 13)),
             shape = 21, fill = "white", size = 1.7, stroke = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~keyword, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#2A9D8F", "#6C5CE7", "#E76F51")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Google Trends index (0–100)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "none", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())





Figure 1: Weekly Google search-interest index. Lines are the website CSV; open points are every thirteenth gtrendsR observation. Exact overlap means the two pulls matched in this run.




After mapping the website’s <1 cells to zero, all 783 aligned observations were identical: mean absolute difference 0, maximum difference 0, and therefore no direction of difference. The raw files are still structurally different: the website is wide, uses Week and <1, and puts the category in a preamble; R is long and adds query metadata to every row. This is a result of these particular pulls, not a guarantee.
Google Trends is not a count. Google says it samples searches, divides each point by total searches for its time and geography, and rescales within the query from 0 to 100. Thus 100 is the query’s peak relative interest; 0 generally means too little volume to report, not necessarily no searches. Google also cautions that Trends is not polling and that a spike does not mean a topic is “winning” (Google Trends FAQ).

title: Assignment 2: Google Trends, Two Ways
text:
Sensitivity and method choice
Removing Kamala Harris and rerunning the five-year website query changed 67 of 522 remaining observations (12.8%). Every changed cell rose in the two-term pull; the largest increase was four index points. This happens because the sample and the within-query normalization are recomputed, so values are comparable only inside the query that produced them.
Harris and Kamala Harris were not the same series: in a joint R query none of their 261 weekly values matched; the mean absolute gap was 7.46 and the maximum was 35 index points. A search term measures the literal words entered, whereas a Google Trends topic groups searches for a concept across wording and languages (Google’s term-versus-topic guide). The bare surname therefore does not isolate the intended person.
The website is transparent to inspect but manual: its interest-over-time CSV records the category plus term/geography labels, while my separate query log had to preserve the time window, search type, term-versus-topic choice, and pull time. The R output records keyword, geo, time, gprop, and category in every row and scales to many scripted terms, countries, and repetitions. Neither route guarantees identical future values, but R makes the procedure far easier to regenerate. It is also fragile: gtrendsR depends on an unofficial endpoint, so rate limits or a changed response can break a call; my first website load returned HTTP 429 before a retry succeeded. I cache the first success, retain the raw RDS/CSV, and check row counts, date ranges, and missing values.
With onlyInterest = FALSE, names(tct) returned interest_over_time plus interest_by_country, interest_by_region, interest_by_dma, interest_by_city, related_topics, and related_queries. The single website chart download contained only the first; the other six were absent. The package documents these list-based results and the onlyInterest switch (gtrendsR reference manual).
I also completed and cached the required extensions: Taylor Swift over time = "all", the same term in Great Britain, the term across c("US", "GB", "TW"), and Taylor Swift, Beyonce, and Adele worldwide.
Finally, two identical Federal Reserve R calls returned the same 93 daily values in this run. Because Google describes Trends as sampled data with small statistical noise, equality once does not establish stability. Any reported finding should archive its exact pull, be checked with repetitions, and avoid overinterpreting small differences (Google Trends FAQ).
The complete cached workflow is in code/gtrendsR01.R; derived comparisons are produced by code/analyze_trends.R.
